content.text: Before writing a single line of HTML or JavaScript, every great web developer understands *how the internet actually works*. This section strips away the magic of frameworks to reveal the real protocols, packets, and pipelines that power every website on Earth. Think of this as your X-ray vision into the web.

content.title: Why This Matters
content.text: Developers who understand DNS, TCP, and the browser rendering pipeline debug 10× faster and build more performant apps. This knowledge separates juniors from seniors.
0.1 How the Internet Works — The Full Journey

The internet is a global network of billions of physically interconnected computers. Data travels across **fiber-optic cables** (light pulses at 200,000 km/s), **satellite transceivers** (high latency, global reach), and **copper telephone wires** (DSL). When data is sent, it is broken into **small packets** (typically 1500 bytes max — called the MTU: Maximum Transmission Unit) and each packet is independently routed through intermediate nodes using the IP protocol.

Think of the internet like a postal system: your letter (data) is split into postcards (packets), each postcard travels independently through different post offices (routers), and they are reassembled at the destination (your browser). If a postcard gets lost, the sender re-mails only that one.
What Happens When You Type a URL? (Step by Step)
When you type `https://learnxchain.com/index.html` into your browser and press Enter, a precise 8-step sequence fires:

items: **URL Parsing**: The browser splits the URL into components: protocol (`https`), hostname (`learnxchain.com`), port (`443` default for HTTPS), path (`/index.html`), and optional query string/fragment.
**Cache Check**: The browser checks its DNS cache, then the OS cache, then the router cache for a known IP address for the hostname.

**DNS Lookup**: If not cached, a DNS resolver (usually your ISP's) traverses the DNS hierarchy: Root Server → TLD Server (.com) → Authoritative Name Server → returns IP address (e.g., `104.26.2.22`). This takes 20–120ms.
**TCP Connection (3-Way Handshake)**: The browser opens a TCP connection on port 443 using SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK packets. This takes 1 RTT (Round-Trip Time).
**TLS Handshake**: For HTTPS, the client and server negotiate TLS version, cipher suites, and session keys by verifying the server's SSL certificate. TLS 1.3 does this in 1 RTT.
**HTTP Request**: The browser sends `GET /index.html HTTP/2` with headers (Host, Accept, Cookie, User-Agent).
**Server Processing**: NGINX receives the request, passes it to the app server, which queries a database if needed, and returns `200 OK` with the HTML body.
**Browser Rendering**: HTML is parsed → DOM built → CSS parsed → CSSOM built → Render Tree constructed → Layout → Paint → Composite layers → display on screen.

content.text: 0.2 DNS & Networking Protocols Deep Dive

**DNS (Domain Name System)** is the phone book of the internet. It maps human-readable hostnames like `google.com` to machine-routable IP addresses like `142.250.80.46`. DNS uses **UDP port 53** for fast, connectionless queries. Responses are cached using TTL (Time-To-Live) values set by domain owners.
DNS Record Types — Complete Reference

rows: Start of Authority — primary zone info

content.text: TCP vs UDP — The Core Transport Layer Choice

At Layer 4 (Transport Layer) of the OSI model, all internet traffic uses either **TCP** (reliable, ordered, connection-based) or **UDP** (fast, fire-and-forget). The right choice depends on whether you need guaranteed delivery or raw speed.

rows: ❌ Packets may be lost, duplicated, or arrive out of order
Faster — minimal headers = 8 bytes, no handshake
HTTP/HTTPS, SSH, FTP, database connections, email
DNS, live video/audio streaming, VoIP, gaming, WebRTC

content.title: HTTP/3 Uses UDP!
content.text: HTTP/3 (used by 30%+ of the web) is built on QUIC, a protocol that runs over UDP. QUIC implements its own reliability, ordering, and encryption — getting UDP's speed with TCP's guarantees. It eliminates 'head-of-line blocking' that plagued HTTP/2.
HTTP vs HTTPS & SSL/TLS In Depth

**HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol) transmits data as **plain text**. Anyone on your network (your router, ISP, or a hacker on the same WiFi) can read your data with a packet sniffer like Wireshark. **HTTPS** wraps HTTP inside **TLS (Transport Layer Security)** — an encryption layer that makes data unreadable to third parties.

items: **Confidentiality**: TLS encrypts data so only the intended recipient can read it.
**Integrity**: A MAC (Message Authentication Code) ensures data wasn't tampered with in transit.
**Authentication**: The server's SSL Certificate (signed by a trusted CA like Let's Encrypt) proves the server is who it claims to be, preventing impersonation.
**SEO Boost**: Google ranks HTTPS sites higher. Chrome marks HTTP sites as 'Not Secure'.

content.title: TLS 1.3 Speed Optimization
content.text: TLS 1.3 reduces the handshake from 2 RTTs to 1 RTT by combining key exchange and cipher negotiation. It also supports '0-RTT resumption' for returning users — no handshake overhead at all on repeat visits.
0.3 Browser Rendering Pipeline — Critical Path

Once the browser receives the raw HTML bytes from the server, the **rendering engine** (Blink in Chrome/Edge, Gecko in Firefox, WebKit in Safari) executes the **Critical Rendering Path (CRP)** — a precise sequence of steps to paint pixels on screen.

items: **Bytes → Characters**: HTML bytes decoded using charset (UTF-8) into individual characters.
**Characters → Tokens**: HTML Parser tokenizes characters into start tags, end tags, attributes, and text nodes.
**Tokens → Nodes**: Each token becomes a Node object (HTMLElement, TextNode, CommentNode).
**Nodes → DOM Tree**: Nodes are linked into a parent-child tree — the Document Object Model.
**CSS → CSSOM**: CSS files are parsed into the CSS Object Model — a parallel tree of style rules.
**DOM + CSSOM → Render Tree**: The DOM and CSSOM are combined. Display:none elements are excluded. Each visible node gets its computed styles.
**Layout (Reflow)**: The browser calculates the exact position (x, y) and size (width, height) of every element on the viewport.
**Paint**: Rendering instructions (fill, stroke, text, shadow) are recorded for each layer.
**Composite**: The GPU composites layers together. CSS transforms and opacity changes happen here — GPU-accelerated and very fast.

content.title: Performance Warning: Avoid Layout Thrashing
content.text: Reading layout properties (offsetWidth, getBoundingClientRect) then writing style in a loop forces repeated reflows — a 'layout thrash'. Always batch reads, then batch writes. Use CSS transforms (translateX) instead of changing top/left — they skip Layout and go straight to Composite (GPU layer).
0.4 Web Infrastructure: Servers, CDNs & Caching

A **Web Server** (like NGINX or Caddy) handles HTTP connections, serves static files, and acts as a **reverse proxy** — forwarding dynamic requests to an application server (Node.js, Python, Java). A **CDN (Content Delivery Network)** like Cloudflare or AWS CloudFront maintains hundreds of **edge nodes** worldwide, caching your static assets (JS, CSS, images) close to users — reducing latency from 300ms to under 10ms.
Complete Cache-Control Header Reference

rows: Never cache — re-fetch fresh copy every time
Bank data, health records, checkout pages
Cache it, but always revalidate with server (ETag check) before serving
Pages that change frequently but can tolerate stale briefly
Cache for 1 year, never re-check. `immutable` tells browser the content will never change
Cache on the user's browser only (not on CDNs), for 1 hour
Serve stale copy immediately, re-fetch in background within 60s
API responses where slight staleness is acceptable

content.title: Cache Busting Strategy
content.text: Set `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` on your assets — but include a content hash in the filename (e.g., `main.a3f9bc.js`). When the code changes, Vite/Webpack generates a new hash, forcing browsers to download the new file while still getting maximum caching for unchanged files.
0.5 Web State & Storage Mechanisms

HTTP is a **stateless protocol** — each request is completely independent. The server has no memory of previous requests. To persist state across requests (login sessions, user preferences, shopping carts), developers use several storage mechanisms:

rows: Session tokens, auth (set HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite=Strict)
User preferences, draft data, cached responses
Wizard step data, temporary form state
Offline apps, large structured data, PWAs

content.text: Interview Questions: Computer Science Foundations

content.question: Explain the difference between LocalStorage and Cookies. When would you use each?
content.answer:
LocalStorage (5-10MB) stores data client-side only — it is never automatically sent to the server. Use it for UI preferences (dark mode, language), cached API responses, or draft content.

Cookies (4KB) are sent automatically with every HTTP request to the domain. If configured with `HttpOnly`, JS cannot access them — making them safe against XSS. Use `Secure` (HTTPS only) and `SameSite=Strict` (block CSRF). Use cookies for authentication session tokens.

Key rule: Never store sensitive data (passwords, tokens) in LocalStorage. Always use HttpOnly cookies for auth.

content.question: What is the difference between TCP's 3-way handshake and the TLS handshake?
content.answer:
TCP 3-way handshake (Transport Layer — Layer 4):
1. Client → Server: SYN (sequence number=100)
2. Server → Client: SYN-ACK (seq=200, ack=101)
3. Client → Server: ACK (ack=201)
This establishes a reliable, ordered connection. It does NOT encrypt anything.

TLS handshake (Presentation Layer — Layer 6, happens AFTER TCP):
1. Client Hello: Supported TLS versions + cipher suites
2. Server Hello: Chosen cipher + SSL Certificate
3. Client verifies certificate against trusted CAs
4. Key exchange (ECDHE): Both sides compute shared secret
5. Session keys derived. Encrypted channel begins.

TLS 1.3 compresses this to 1 RTT vs TLS 1.2's 2 RTTs.

content.text: HTML is not just tags — it is a **contract between your content, search engines, and assistive technologies**. Modern HTML written correctly is semantic, accessible, and SEO-optimized by default. This chapter covers everything from document structure to advanced form validation, ARIA landmarks, and Web Components.
1.1 HTML Document Structure — The Skeleton
Every HTML page starts with a DOCTYPE declaration and follows a strict hierarchy. Understanding this structure is foundational before writing any content.

content.text: 1.2 Semantic HTML — Meaning Over Markup

**Semantic elements** clearly describe their *meaning* to both the browser and developer tools. They improve SEO (search engines weight semantic content), accessibility (screen readers announce element roles), and developer experience (self-documenting code). The rule: **use the element whose name matches the content's purpose**.

rows: Site or section header. Contains logo, nav, search.
Primary content of the page (only one per page!)
Self-contained, independently distributable content (blog post, tweet, product card)
Thematic grouping of related content with its own heading
Footer of a page or section (copyright, links)
Self-contained content with optional caption (images, code, charts)

content.title: The Div Soup Anti-Pattern
content.text: Overusing <div> and <span> for everything is called 'div soup' — it creates inaccessible, non-semantic markup that screen readers cannot interpret and search engines cannot understand. Always reach for the most specific semantic element first.
1.3 Accessibility (a11y) — Building for Everyone

**Accessibility (a11y)** means making websites usable by people with visual, motor, auditory, and cognitive disabilities. It's not optional — the ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act) mandates it for many organizations. Accessible sites also rank higher in SEO and convert better with all users.
WCAG 2.1 Compliance Checklist (Level AA)

items: **Keyboard Navigation**: All interactive elements (links, buttons, forms, modals) must be reachable via `Tab` and operable via `Enter`/`Space`. No keyboard traps.
**Focus Indicators**: Visible focus rings on all focusable elements. Never use `outline: none` without a custom focus style replacement.
**Color Contrast**: Text must have a minimum 4.5:1 contrast ratio against background (3:1 for large text ≥18px). Test with WebAIM Contrast Checker.
**Alternative Text**: All meaningful images need descriptive `alt` text. Decorative images use `alt=""` (empty, not omitted).
**Form Labels**: Every input must have a visible `<label>` associated via `for`/`id` matching, or `aria-label` for icon-only controls.
**Error Messages**: Form errors must be announced to screen readers using `role="alert"` or `aria-live="polite"`.
**Heading Hierarchy**: Use `<h1>` → `<h2>` → `<h3>` in logical order. Never skip levels (h1 → h3). Only one `<h1>` per page.
**Link Purpose**: Link text must be descriptive. Never use 'click here' or 'read more' alone — screen readers list all links out of context.
**Language Attribute**: `<html lang='en'>` tells assistive tech the page language for correct pronunciation.
**Responsive/Zoomable**: Content must be usable at 200% zoom. No disabling of pinch-to-zoom.

Forms are how users interact with your application. HTML5 provides **built-in validation** that works without JavaScript, improves performance, and is more accessible than custom JS validators.

content.text: 1.6 HTML Performance Best Practices

items: **Place `<script>` before `</body>` or use `defer`/`async`** — Inline scripts block HTML parsing. `defer` downloads in parallel, executes after parsing. `async` downloads in parallel, executes immediately when ready.
**Use `<link rel='preload'>` for critical resources** — Fonts, hero images, and critical JS should be preloaded to reduce LCP (Largest Contentful Paint).
**Lazy-load off-screen images**: `` — Built into browsers, defers loading until user scrolls near the image.
**Use `<picture>` for responsive images** — Serve WebP to modern browsers, JPEG as fallback. Serve appropriately-sized images using `srcset` and `sizes`.
**Use `loading='lazy'` on iframes** — Especially for YouTube embeds, maps, and third-party widgets.
**Preconnect to external origins**: `<link rel='preconnect' href='https://fonts.googleapis.com'>` — Establishes the TCP+TLS connection before the resource is actually needed.

content.text: Interview Questions: HTML Masterclass

content.question: What is the difference between `defer` and `async` attributes on a `<script>` tag?
content.answer:
Both attributes allow the HTML parser to continue building the DOM while the script downloads in parallel — preventing render-blocking.

`async`: Script executes immediately when downloaded, regardless of where the parser is. Order is not guaranteed. Use for independent scripts like analytics where order and DOM access don't matter.

`defer`: Script executes after the full HTML document is parsed, in the order they appear in the HTML. Use for app scripts that depend on the DOM being ready.

Neither attribute works on inline <script> tags — only on external scripts with a src attribute.

content.question: What is the difference between `id` and `class` attributes in HTML?
content.answer:
`id` must be UNIQUE per page — only one element can have a given id. It creates the highest specificity in CSS (0,1,0,0) and is targeted with `#id` in CSS and `document.getElementById()` in JS. Use for page landmarks (main navigation, main content area).

`class` can be reused on multiple elements. It has lower specificity (0,0,1,0) and is targeted with `.className` in CSS and `querySelectorAll()` in JS. Use for reusable component styles.

In modern web dev, avoid id selectors in CSS — they make styles hard to override. Prefer class-based styling with BEM methodology.

content.question: What is the Document Object Model (DOM) and how is it different from HTML?
content.answer:
HTML is a text file — a string of markup that you write. The DOM is the live, in-memory tree of objects that the browser builds from parsing that HTML.

The DOM is a programming interface: you can read it (document.querySelector('.btn').textContent), modify it (element.classList.add('active')), and delete from it (element.remove()). These changes update what's displayed on screen in real-time.

Key difference: If your HTML has an error (unclosed tag), the browser may auto-correct it in the DOM. The DOM represents the browser's interpretation, not your raw HTML text. DevTools Elements panel shows the DOM, not your source HTML.

content.text: CSS is the language that transforms raw HTML structure into beautiful, responsive, animated interfaces. Mastering CSS means understanding the **cascade**, **specificity**, **layout engines**, and the **GPU-accelerated animation pipeline**. This chapter gives you complete command over visual design — from box models to complex grid layouts to dark mode theming.
2.1 The CSS Cascade — How Browsers Decide What Wins
When multiple CSS rules target the same element with the same property, the browser must determine which one wins. This decision follows a **cascade** of 4 criteria in order:

items: **Origin & Importance**: `!important` rules > Author styles > User Agent (browser default) styles
**Specificity**: Higher specificity score wins (see table below)
**Order of Appearance**: When specificity ties, the *last* rule in source order wins
**Inheritance**: If no rule applies, some properties (color, font-size) inherit from parent elements

content.text: CSS Specificity Score Table
Specificity is calculated as a 4-column score `[Importance, ID, Class/Pseudo-class/Attr, Element]`. Higher leftmost column wins.

content.title: Specificity Trap
content.text: Avoid using ID selectors in CSS — they're almost impossible to override without !important. Stick to class selectors. If you need to override a library's styles, use a more specific class chain: `.my-app .component .element {}` instead of `!important`.
2.2 The CSS Box Model — Every Element is a Box

Every HTML element is rendered as a rectangular **box**. The box has 4 layers from inside out: **Content → Padding → Border → Margin**. Understanding this model is critical for accurate layout calculations.

content.title: Always Use border-box

content.text: 2.3 Flexbox — One-Dimensional Layouts

Flexbox (Flexible Box Layout) is the perfect tool for **one-dimensional layouts** — arranging items in a row OR column. It excels at: navbars, centering elements, distributing space between cards, aligning button groups, and building responsive sidebars.
2.4 CSS Grid — Two-Dimensional Layouts

CSS Grid is the most powerful layout system in CSS. Unlike Flexbox (1D), Grid controls **both rows and columns simultaneously**. Use it for: page layouts, dashboards, image galleries, card grids, and any complex 2D arrangement.

content.title: Flexbox vs Grid Decision Guide
content.text:
Use FLEXBOX when: laying out items in a single row or column, centering content, distributing navigation items, or when item sizes determine the layout.

Use GRID when: you need to control both rows AND columns, creating page-level layouts (sidebar + main + header), image galleries, or when the layout determines item sizes.
2.5 CSS Variables & Design Systems

**CSS Custom Properties** (CSS variables) are one of the most powerful features of modern CSS. They enable design systems, dynamic theming (dark/light mode), and component customization without JavaScript.
2.6 CSS Animations & Transitions

Animations make interfaces feel alive. CSS provides two animation systems: **transitions** (simple A→B state changes triggered by events) and **keyframe animations** (complex multi-step sequences that run automatically).
2.7 CSS Architecture & BEM Methodology

**BEM (Block, Element, Modifier)** is a CSS naming methodology that prevents style conflicts in large codebases. It creates component-scoped styles without Shadow DOM, making CSS predictable and scalable across teams.
2.8 Responsive Design & Media Queries

Responsive design ensures your UI works on screens from 320px (small phones) to 2560px+ (4K monitors). Use a **mobile-first** approach: write base styles for mobile, then use `min-width` breakpoints to add complexity for larger screens.
Interview Questions: CSS Mastery

content.question: What is the difference between position: relative, absolute, fixed, and sticky?
content.answer:
`relative`: Element stays in normal flow. Can be offset with top/left/right/bottom (relative to its own original position). Creates a containing block for absolute children.

`absolute`: Removed from normal flow. Positioned relative to its nearest ancestor with position !== static. Use for dropdowns, tooltips, overlays.

`fixed`: Removed from normal flow. Positioned relative to the VIEWPORT — doesn't scroll with the page. Use for sticky headers, floating buttons, cookie banners.

`sticky`: Hybrid — stays in normal flow until it hits a scroll threshold, then acts like `fixed`. Use for section headings that stick while their section is visible, or table headers.

content.text: JavaScript is the only programming language that runs natively in every web browser on Earth. Understanding JavaScript at a deep level — its **execution model**, **type system**, **prototype chain**, **closures**, and **asynchronous runtime** — is the foundation of all modern web development. This chapter builds that foundation from the ground up.
3.1 JavaScript Fundamentals — Variables, Types & Scope

JavaScript is a **dynamically typed**, **interpreted** (JIT-compiled in V8), **prototype-based**, **single-threaded** language with a **non-blocking event loop**. Let's break down each of these characteristics.
Variables: var vs let vs const

rows: Hoisted but in TDZ (Temporal Dead Zone)
❌ Avoid — use in legacy code only

content.text: 3.2 Functions — First-Class Citizens

In JavaScript, functions are **first-class objects** — they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, returned from other functions, and stored in arrays. This enables powerful patterns like **callbacks**, **closures**, **higher-order functions**, and **currying**.
3.3 Objects, Prototypes & ES6 Classes

JavaScript is **prototype-based** — objects inherit from other objects via a prototype chain. ES6 `class` syntax is syntactic sugar over this prototype system — there are no real 'classes' in JavaScript, only objects linked via prototypes.
3.4 Array Methods — The Complete Toolkit
Mastering array methods is essential for writing functional, readable JavaScript. These methods are the backbone of data transformation in React and backend APIs.
3.5 DOM Manipulation — From Static to Interactive

The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's in-memory representation of your HTML. JavaScript can read, modify, create, and delete DOM nodes to create interactive experiences. Every React or Vue framework ultimately calls these browser APIs under the hood.
Interview Questions: JavaScript

content.question: What is a closure? Give a real-world use case.
content.answer:
A closure is when an inner function retains access to variables from its outer (enclosing) function's scope, even after the outer function has returned. The inner function 'closes over' the outer scope.

Real-world use cases:
1. Data privacy / encapsulation: module pattern hides private state
2. Factory functions: create specialized functions with pre-set arguments (makeMultiplier(5))
3. Memoization: cache function results using a closed-over Map
4. React hooks: useState, useEffect closures capture the component's scope
5. Event handlers: click handlers close over element references and state

Example:
function makeAdder(x) {
  return (y) => x + y;  // closes over x
}
const add5 = makeAdder(5);
add5(3); // 8 — x is still accessible

content.question: What is the difference between `==` and `===` in JavaScript?
content.answer:
`==` (Abstract Equality): Performs type coercion before comparing. JavaScript converts operands to the same type, then compares values.
0 == false → true (false coerces to 0)
'' == false → true
null == undefined → true
1 == '1' → true

`===` (Strict Equality): No type coercion. Both type AND value must match.
0 === false → false (different types)
1 === '1' → false (different types)
null === undefined → false

Always use === in production code. The only exception: if (value == null) catches both null and undefined in one check — a deliberate, well-known pattern.

content.question: Explain hoisting in JavaScript.
content.answer:
Hoisting is JavaScript's behavior of moving declarations to the top of their scope before code execution. But only DECLARATIONS are hoisted — not initializations.

var declarations: Hoisted and initialized to undefined.
console.log(x); // undefined (not ReferenceError!)
var x = 5;

function declarations: Fully hoisted — can be called before definition.
greet(); // Works!
function greet() { return 'hi'; }

let/const: Hoisted but NOT initialized — accessing before declaration throws ReferenceError (Temporal Dead Zone).
console.log(y); // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'y' before initialization
let y = 10;

Best practice: Always declare variables at the top of their scope. Use const/let, never var.

content.text: This chapter covers the advanced JavaScript concepts that separate competent developers from outstanding ones: **prototypal inheritance**, **design patterns**, **memory management**, **the `this` keyword**, **iterators/generators**, and **ES2023+ features**.
4.1 The `this` Keyword — Context Binding

`this` is one of JavaScript's most confusing concepts. Unlike other languages, `this` in JavaScript is determined at **call time** — not at definition time. There are 4 binding rules in order of priority:

items: **new binding**: `new Constructor()` — `this` is the newly created object
**Explicit binding**: `.call(obj)`, `.apply(obj)`, `.bind(obj)` — `this` is explicitly set
**Implicit binding**: `obj.method()` — `this` is the object before the dot
**Default binding**: `func()` — `this` is `undefined` in strict mode, `global` in non-strict

content.text: 4.2 JavaScript Design Patterns
Design patterns are proven, reusable solutions to common software design problems. Knowing when and how to apply them makes your code more maintainable, testable, and scalable.
4.3 Memory Management & Avoiding Leaks

JavaScript uses **automatic garbage collection** (mark-and-sweep algorithm). The GC identifies objects that are no longer **reachable** from any root (global, stack frame, event listeners) and frees their memory. Memory leaks occur when you accidentally keep references alive.

content.title: Memory Leak Danger
content.text:
The top 4 sources of memory leaks in JavaScript:

content.text: JavaScript is **single-threaded** — it can only do one thing at a time. Yet we need to make network requests, read files, set timers, and handle user events without freezing the UI. This is achieved through the **Event Loop** — the engine behind all of JavaScript's non-blocking behavior.
5.1 The Event Loop — JavaScript's Heart

The JavaScript runtime consists of: a **Call Stack** (LIFO), a **Heap** (memory allocation), a **Web APIs layer** (browser APIs for setTimeout, fetch, DOM events), a **Microtask Queue** (Promise callbacks), and a **Task Queue** (setTimeout, setInterval callbacks). The Event Loop runs continuously checking: if the Call Stack is empty, it processes the Microtask Queue completely, then takes one task from the Task Queue.
5.2 Promises — Async Programming Done Right

A **Promise** is an object representing the eventual completion (or failure) of an asynchronous operation. It has 3 states: **Pending** (initial), **Fulfilled** (resolved with a value), **Rejected** (failed with a reason). Once settled, a Promise cannot change state.
5.3 Async/Await — The Modern Way

`async/await` is syntactic sugar over Promises that makes asynchronous code look and behave like synchronous code. An `async` function always returns a Promise. `await` pauses execution inside the async function until the Promise settles — without blocking the main thread.
Interview Questions: Async JavaScript

content.question: What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks in the Event Loop?
content.answer:
Macrotasks (Task Queue): setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate, I/O callbacks, UI rendering. Only ONE macrotask is processed per Event Loop iteration.

Microtasks (Microtask Queue): Promise .then/.catch/.finally callbacks, queueMicrotask(), MutationObserver. ALL pending microtasks are processed to completion after each task, BEFORE the next macrotask runs.

Order:
1. Execute current synchronous code
2. Process ALL microtasks (including new microtasks added during this step)
3. Render UI if needed
4. Process ONE macrotask
5. Repeat from step 2

This means: infinitely chaining Promise.resolve() would starve the rendering and setTimeout callbacks!

content.question: What are the differences between Promise.all, Promise.allSettled, Promise.race, and Promise.any?
content.answer:
Promise.all([p1, p2, p3]): Waits for ALL to fulfill. If ANY rejects, immediately rejects. Use when you need all results and any failure should abort.

Promise.allSettled([p1, p2, p3]): Waits for ALL to settle (fulfill or reject). Never rejects. Returns array of {status, value/reason}. Use when you need all results regardless of individual failures.

Promise.race([p1, p2, p3]): Returns first to SETTLE (fulfill or reject). Use for timeout patterns or racing redundant requests.

Promise.any([p1, p2, p3]): Returns first to FULFILL (ignores rejections). Only rejects if ALL reject (AggregateError). Use for fallback strategies — fastest successful result wins.

content.text: Node.js brings JavaScript to the **server side** — enabling full-stack development in a single language. Built on Chrome's V8 engine with a non-blocking, event-driven architecture, Node.js excels at I/O-intensive tasks: APIs, real-time chat, stream processing, and microservices.
6.1 Node.js Architecture & Module System

Node.js uses **libuv** — a C library — to implement its event loop, thread pool, and non-blocking I/O. The main thread runs JavaScript, while libuv handles OS operations (file system, DNS, crypto) on a thread pool. This is how Node.js achieves non-blocking I/O without multi-threading in JavaScript.
CommonJS vs ES Modules
6.2 Node.js Streams — Processing Large Data Efficiently

content.title: Why Streams Matter
content.text: Reading a 2GB CSV file with fs.readFile() loads it all into memory — potentially crashing your server. Streams read data in chunks (16KB default), process each chunk, and discard it — using constant memory regardless of file size.
6.3 Node.js Event System

content.question: What is the Node.js Event Loop and how is it different from the browser's?
content.answer:
Node.js Event Loop phases (libuv):
1. timers: executes setTimeout/setInterval callbacks
2. pending callbacks: OS I/O error callbacks
3. idle, prepare: internal use
4. poll: retrieve new I/O events (waits here if nothing else pending)
5. check: setImmediate() callbacks
6. close callbacks: socket.on('close') etc.

Between each phase: microtasks (Promise callbacks) and process.nextTick() are drained completely.

process.nextTick() runs BEFORE Promise microtasks — highest priority.

Browser Event Loop differences:
- No setImmediate (use setTimeout(fn, 0) instead)
- No process.nextTick
- Browser adds a rendering phase between tasks
- Browser API callbacks (click, fetch) go to macrotask queue
- Both drain microtask queue after each macrotask

content.question: What is middleware in Express.js and how does it work?
content.answer:
Middleware are functions that have access to (req, res, next) and execute in sequence for every matching request. They form a pipeline — each middleware either ends the request cycle (sends a response) or calls next() to pass control to the next middleware.

Types:
1. Application-level: app.use(fn) — runs for all routes
2. Router-level: router.use(fn) — runs for routes in that router
3. Error-handling: (err, req, res, next) — 4 params, only runs on errors
4. Built-in: express.json(), express.static()
5. Third-party: helmet, cors, morgan, compression

Order matters: middleware executes in the order registered. Always put error handlers LAST. Put security middleware (helmet, cors, rateLimit) FIRST.

content.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
content.answer:
Authentication (AuthN): Verifying IDENTITY — 'Who are you?'
Validates credentials (email+password, OAuth token, API key, certificate). Result: a verified user identity.

Authorization (AuthZ): Verifying PERMISSIONS — 'What are you allowed to do?'
Checks if the authenticated user has permission to perform a specific action on a resource. Result: access granted or forbidden (403).

In an Express app:
1. authenticate middleware: validates JWT, attaches user to req.user
2. authorize('admin') middleware: checks req.user.role === 'admin'

Common auth patterns:
- JWT (stateless): token contains claims, server validates signature
- Sessions (stateful): server stores session, sends session ID cookie
- OAuth 2.0: delegate auth to Google/GitHub (for social login)
- API Keys: for machine-to-machine communication

content.text: Every web application ultimately persists and retrieves data. The choice of database — **relational vs document**, **normalized vs denormalized**, **indexed vs unindexed** — determines your application's performance at scale. This chapter covers everything from SQL fundamentals to indexing strategies, transactions, and NoSQL trade-offs.
8.1 Relational Databases & SQL

**Relational databases** store data in **tables** (rows and columns) with predefined schemas. Relationships between tables are defined using **foreign keys**. SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for querying and manipulating relational data.
Database Design — Normalization
**Normalization** is the process of organizing a database to reduce data redundancy and improve integrity. The three most important Normal Forms (NF) are:

items: **1NF (First Normal Form)**: Each column contains atomic (indivisible) values. No repeating groups. Each row is unique (has a primary key).
**2NF (Second Normal Form)**: Must be in 1NF. Every non-key column must depend on the ENTIRE primary key (no partial dependencies). Eliminates redundancy from composite keys.
**3NF (Third Normal Form)**: Must be in 2NF. No transitive dependencies — non-key columns must not depend on other non-key columns. Move dependent data to a separate table.

codeMap.sql:
-- ═══ SCHEMA DESIGN — Normalized ═══
CREATE TABLE users (
  id          UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email       VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name        VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  password_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
  role        VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'student'
                CHECK (role IN ('student', 'instructor', 'admin')),
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
  updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE courses (
  id            UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  title         VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
  description   TEXT,
  price         DECIMAL(8,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (price >= 0),
  level         VARCHAR(20) CHECK (level IN ('beginner', 'intermediate', 'advanced')),
  instructor_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  published_at  TIMESTAMPTZ,
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE enrollments (
  id          UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  course_id   UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES courses(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  enrolled_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
  completed_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
  UNIQUE(user_id, course_id)  -- prevent duplicate enrollments
);

-- ═══ INDEXES — the secret to fast queries ═══
CREATE INDEX idx_courses_instructor ON courses(instructor_id);  -- FK lookups
CREATE INDEX idx_courses_level ON courses(level);               -- filter by level
CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_user ON enrollments(user_id);      -- user's courses
CREATE INDEX idx_courses_published ON courses(published_at DESC)  -- ordering
  WHERE published_at IS NOT NULL;  -- partial index (only published!)
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);                   -- login lookup

-- ═══ SQL QUERIES — from basic to advanced ═══

-- Simple SELECT with filtering
SELECT title, price, level
FROM courses
WHERE level = 'beginner' AND price < 50
ORDER BY price ASC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 0;

-- JOIN — get courses with instructor names
SELECT 
  c.title,
  c.price,
  u.name AS instructor_name,
  COUNT(e.id) AS enrolled_count
FROM courses c
INNER JOIN users u ON c.instructor_id = u.id
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.title, c.price, u.name
HAVING COUNT(e.id) > 10
ORDER BY enrolled_count DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Subquery — users enrolled in 3+ courses
SELECT name, email
FROM users
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT user_id
  FROM enrollments
  GROUP BY user_id
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
);

-- CTE (Common Table Expression) — much more readable!
WITH popular_courses AS (
  SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS enrollment_count
  FROM enrollments
  GROUP BY course_id
  HAVING COUNT(*) > 100
),
recent_enrollments AS (
  SELECT * FROM enrollments
  WHERE enrolled_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
)
SELECT c.title, pc.enrollment_count
FROM popular_courses pc
JOIN courses c ON c.id = pc.course_id
WHERE c.id IN (SELECT course_id FROM recent_enrollments);

content.text: 8.2 Database Indexing — The Performance Secret

A database **index** is a separate data structure (usually a **B-Tree**) that enables the database to find rows matching a WHERE condition in O(log n) time instead of O(n) full-table scan. Proper indexing is the most impactful performance optimization for most applications.

content.title: Index Selectivity Warning
content.text: Indexes are most beneficial on high-selectivity columns (columns with many unique values like email, UUID, name). A boolean `is_active` column has only 2 values — an index on it may be slower than a full scan (the optimizer ignores it). Compound indexes must match the query's WHERE clause order — (user_id, course_id) won't be used by a query filtering only on course_id.

codeMap.sql:
-- ═══ INDEX TYPES ═══

-- B-Tree (default) — equality and range queries, sorting
CREATE INDEX idx_price ON courses(price);  -- WHERE price < 50, ORDER BY price

-- Composite B-Tree — multiple columns (order matters!)
CREATE INDEX idx_user_course ON enrollments(user_id, course_id);
-- Used for: WHERE user_id = ? AND course_id = ?
-- Used for: WHERE user_id = ?  (leading column)
-- NOT used for: WHERE course_id = ?  (not leading)

-- Partial index — only index rows matching a condition
CREATE INDEX idx_published_courses ON courses(created_at DESC)
WHERE published_at IS NOT NULL AND is_deleted = false;
-- Smaller index, faster queries for this specific filter

-- Covering index — includes all columns the query needs
CREATE INDEX idx_course_cover ON courses(level, price)
INCLUDE (title, instructor_id);
-- Query can be answered from index alone (no table access!)

-- Full-text search index
CREATE INDEX idx_course_search ON courses
USING GIN(to_tsvector('english', title || ' ' || description));

-- Search query with ranking
SELECT title, ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', title), query) AS rank
FROM courses, to_tsquery('english', 'javascript & react') query
WHERE to_tsvector('english', title) @@ query
ORDER BY rank DESC;

-- ═══ QUERY ANALYSIS ═══
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM courses WHERE level = 'beginner';
-- Look for: Seq Scan (bad for large tables) vs Index Scan (good)
-- Also check: rows estimate vs actual rows, execution time

content.text: 8.3 ACID Transactions
**ACID** properties guarantee database reliability even when failures occur (crashes, network errors, concurrent access).

rows: All operations in a transaction succeed, or ALL are rolled back — no partial updates
Bank transfer: debit fails → credit is also rolled back
Transaction brings DB from one valid state to another. Constraints never violated.
Can't enroll in a course that doesn't exist (FK constraint)
Concurrent transactions don't see each other's intermediate states
Two users can't buy the last seat simultaneously
Committed transactions survive crashes — written to disk (WAL log)
Payment committed at 2:00 PM is still there after server restart at 2:01 PM

content.text: Interview Questions: Databases

content.question: What is the N+1 query problem and how do you fix it?
What is database indexing? What are the trade-offs of adding too many indexes?
content.answer:
An index is a separate data structure (B-Tree by default) that stores a sorted copy of one or more columns with pointers to the original table rows. It speeds up SELECT queries from O(n) to O(log n).

Trade-offs of too many indexes:
1. Write penalty: Every INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE must also update ALL indexes on the table — can be 2-5x slower writes
2. Storage: Each index takes disk space — a large table with 10 indexes might use more space for indexes than data
3. Memory: Active indexes are loaded into buffer pool (RAM) — too many compete for memory
4. Query planner overhead: Optimizer must evaluate more index options for each query

Rule: Create indexes based on actual slow queries (from EXPLAIN ANALYZE or slow query log). Don't pre-optimize — index when needed.

content.text: React is the most widely used UI library in the world. Built on the **Virtual DOM**, **unidirectional data flow**, and a **component-based architecture**, React enables building complex, interactive UIs with predictable state management. This chapter covers React from fundamentals to production patterns.
9.1 React Fundamentals — Components, Props & JSX

React UIs are built from **components** — reusable, independent pieces of UI. Each component is a JavaScript function that takes **props** (input data) and returns **JSX** (HTML-like syntax that compiles to `React.createElement()` calls).
9.2 useState & useEffect — Core Hooks
9.3 Custom Hooks — Reusable Logic

9.4 State Management — Context API & External Stores

content.question: What is the Virtual DOM and how does React's reconciliation algorithm work?
content.answer:
The Virtual DOM (VDOM) is a lightweight in-memory JavaScript representation of the real DOM tree. React maintains this tree and performs a 'diffing' algorithm to determine the minimal set of real DOM operations needed.

Reconciliation process:
1. State/prop change triggers re-render of component subtree
2. React calls the component function, generating a new VDOM tree
3. React 'diffs' the new tree against the previous tree (fiber architecture)
4. Differences are collected into a list of patches (insertions, updates, deletions)
5. React applies ONLY the patches to the real DOM (batched, asynchronous in React 18)

Key rules:
- Elements of different types produce completely new trees (no reuse)
- Elements of the same type are updated in-place
- Lists use `key` prop to identify moved/added/removed items
- Keys must be stable and unique (never use index as key for reorderable lists)

content.question: What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback?
content.answer:
Both are performance optimization hooks that memoize values to prevent unnecessary recalculations on re-renders.

useCallback(fn, deps): Memoizes a FUNCTION reference. Returns the same function instance between renders unless deps change.
Use when: Passing callbacks to child components that use React.memo (prevents re-render when parent re-renders but function hasn't changed). Also for useEffect dependencies.

const handleClick = useCallback(() => {
  setCount(c => c + 1);
}, []);  // stable reference — created once

useMemo(fn, deps): Memoizes a COMPUTED VALUE. Re-runs the function only when deps change.
Use when: Expensive calculations (filtering large arrays, complex transforms) that shouldn't rerun on every render.

const sortedCourses = useMemo(() =>
  courses.sort((a, b) => b.rating - a.rating),
[courses]);  // only re-sort when courses array changes

Key: Don't overuse — the memoization itself has overhead. Profile first.

content.question: What is the difference between `interface` and `type` in TypeScript?
content.answer:
Both define the shape of an object. Key differences:

interface:
- Can be extended: `interface Admin extends User { permissions: string[] }`
- Can be merged (declaration merging): two interfaces with the same name merge
- Better for defining object/class shapes (OOP-style)

type:
- Can represent ANY type: primitives, unions, tuples, mapped types
- Cannot be reopened/merged
- type Result = 'success' | 'error';  // union
- type Point = [number, number];       // tuple
- type Id = string;                    // alias
- type Callback<T> = (arg: T) => void; // generic alias

General rule: Use `interface` for object shapes (especially public APIs), use `type` for everything else (unions, aliases, utility types, complex generics).

content.question: What is the difference between Server Components and Client Components in Next.js App Router?
content.answer:
Server Components (default in App Router):
- Run on the server — never sent to the browser
- Zero JavaScript bundle size contribution
- Can directly access databases, file system, environment secrets
- Can use async/await at component level
- Cannot use: useState, useEffect, event handlers, browser APIs, or Context
- Great for: data fetching, layouts, large components, SEO content

Client Components ('use client' at top of file):
- Run in both server (initial HTML) and browser (hydration)
- Can use all React hooks, event handlers, browser APIs
- Send JavaScript to the browser (increases bundle size)
- Great for: interactive UI, forms, real-time updates, animations

Architecture pattern: Push interactivity to leaf components. Keep the tree as Server Components as much as possible. Compose: <ServerLayout> → <ClientInteractiveWidget />.

content.text: Security is not optional — it's a fundamental requirement. This chapter covers **JWT authentication**, **session management**, **OAuth 2.0 / OIDC**, **password hashing**, **CSRF/XSS prevention**, **SQL injection**, and **security headers** — the complete production security toolkit.
12.1 JWT Authentication — Deep Dive

A **JSON Web Token (JWT)** is a compact, self-contained token that encodes claims (user data) signed with a secret. It enables **stateless authentication** — the server doesn't need to store session data, making it ideal for microservices and horizontal scaling.

A JWT consists of 3 base64url-encoded parts separated by dots: `header.payload.signature`. The **header** specifies the algorithm (RS256 or HS256). The **payload** contains claims (sub, iat, exp, role). The **signature** is `HMAC_SHA256(base64(header) + '.' + base64(payload), secretKey)` — tamper-proof.
12.2 Web Security Vulnerabilities
XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)

**XSS** occurs when an attacker injects malicious JavaScript into your page that executes in other users' browsers. Types: **Stored XSS** (injected into DB, served to all users), **Reflected XSS** (in URL parameters), **DOM-based XSS** (client-side JS uses unsanitized input).
CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)

**CSRF** tricks an authenticated user's browser into sending a request to your API from a malicious third-party website. The browser automatically includes cookies (including session cookies), so the server sees an authenticated request it didn't expect.
SQL Injection
**SQL Injection** occurs when user input is directly concatenated into SQL queries, allowing attackers to manipulate the query logic — reading unauthorized data, deleting tables, or bypassing auth.
Interview Questions: Security

content.question: What security headers should every web application set?
content.answer:
Critical security headers (use `helmet` npm package for Express to set all automatically):

1. Content-Security-Policy: Whitelist trusted script, style, image sources. Prevents XSS.
2. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff — Prevents MIME-type sniffing attacks.
3. X-Frame-Options: DENY — Prevents your page from being embedded in iframes (clickjacking).
4. Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains — Forces HTTPS.
5. Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin — Controls what data is sent in Referer header.
6. Permissions-Policy: Disables access to sensitive browser APIs (camera, microphone, geolocation) that your app doesn't need.
7. Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin — Prevents other sites from loading your resources.

In Express: app.use(helmet()) sets all of these with sensible defaults in one line.

content.text: System design is the art of **architecting scalable, reliable, and maintainable systems**. This chapter covers the fundamental building blocks of large-scale web systems: load balancing, caching, message queues, databases at scale, CDNs, and real-world case studies like designing Twitter, Netflix, and WhatsApp.
13.1 Scalability Fundamentals
**Scalability** is a system's ability to handle growing load without degrading performance. There are two strategies:

items: **Vertical Scaling (Scale Up)**: Upgrade the existing server to a more powerful machine (more CPU, RAM, faster disk). Simple — no code changes. Limited by the maximum hardware available. Single point of failure. Example: upgrading from 4-core to 32-core server.

**Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out)**: Add more servers behind a load balancer. Theoretically unlimited. Requires stateless application design (sessions in Redis, not local memory). More complex — requires distributed systems knowledge. Example: adding 10 more Node.js instances.

**Database Sharding**: Split a large database table across multiple database servers (shards) based on a shard key (e.g., user_id modulo 4). Each shard handles a subset of the data. Enables horizontal database scaling.
**Read Replicas**: One primary database for writes, multiple read-only replicas for reads. 80% of most app traffic is reads — distributing reads dramatically reduces primary load.

content.text: 13.2 Caching — The Performance Multiplier

**Caching** stores expensive computation results or database query results in fast memory (Redis) for subsequent reads. A well-designed cache can reduce database load by 80-90% and reduce API response times from 200ms to under 5ms.
13.3 Message Queues & Event-Driven Architecture

A **message queue** decouples producers (services that create work) from consumers (services that process work). This enables **asynchronous processing**, **load leveling**, **retry mechanisms**, and **service isolation** — the backbone of microservices architecture.
Interview Questions: System Design

content.question: How would you design a URL shortener like bit.ly?
content.answer:
Requirements: Accept long URLs, return short 6-char codes. Handle 100M URLs, 1B reads/day.

API Design:
POST /shorten { url: 'https://...' } → { shortCode: 'abc123' }
GET /{code} → 301 Redirect to original URL

Core Algorithm (Base62 encoding):
1. Assign auto-incrementing ID to each URL (e.g., ID = 12345678)
2. Encode to base62: 12345678 → 'dnh75' (using 0-9, a-z, A-Z alphabet)
3. Store mapping: { code: 'dnh75', url: 'https://...', createdAt, clicks }

Database: PostgreSQL for URL storage. Index on (code) for O(log n) lookup.

Caching: Redis cache for hot URLs (top 20% URLs = 80% of traffic). GET /{code} → check Redis first → fallback to DB.

Scaling: Horizontal web servers behind load balancer. Read replicas for DB. CDN for 301 responses (browser caches redirects for 24h). Counter service for click analytics (async, don't block redirects).

Custom domains: CNAME to our servers, tenant lookup by Host header.

content.text: Shipping code to production reliably, repeatably, and safely is a core engineering skill. This chapter covers **Docker containerization**, **CI/CD pipelines**, **environment management**, **monitoring & alerting**, and **cloud deployment** — everything needed to go from `npm run dev` to production at scale.
14.1 Docker — Containerization

**Docker** packages your application and all its dependencies (runtime, libraries, config) into a **container** — a lightweight, portable, isolated environment that runs identically everywhere: your laptop, CI, staging, and production. Eliminates 'it works on my machine' forever.

codeMap.dockerfile:
# ═══ PRODUCTION-GRADE DOCKERFILE ═══
# Multi-stage build: separate build env from runtime

# Stage 1: Dependencies
FROM node:20-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first (Docker layer cache optimization)
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Stage 2: Builder
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Stage 3: Production runner (smallest possible image)
FROM node:20-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app

# Security: don't run as root
RUN addgroup -g 1001 -S nodejs && adduser -S nextjs -u 1001
USER nextjs

# Copy only what's needed for runtime
COPY --from=deps --chown=nextjs:nodejs /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=builder --chown=nextjs:nodejs /app/.next ./.next
COPY --from=builder --chown=nextjs:nodejs /app/public ./public
COPY --from=builder --chown=nextjs:nodejs /app/package.json ./

# Environment
ENV NODE_ENV=production
ENV PORT=3000

EXPOSE 3000

# Health check — Docker/K8s will restart if this fails
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=10s --start-period=5s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -q -O /dev/null http://localhost:3000/api/health || exit 1

CMD ["npm", "start"]

# docker-compose.yml — Local development environment
version: '3.9'

services:
  app:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.dev
    volumes:
      - .:/app
      - /app/node_modules  # don't override node_modules
    ports:
      - '3000:3000'
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: development
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:password@db:5432/learnxchain
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_started
  
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./init.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: postgres
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password
      POSTGRES_DB: learnxchain
    healthcheck:
      test: ['CMD-SHELL', 'pg_isready -U postgres']
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
  
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: redis-server --save 60 1 --loglevel warning
    volumes:
      - redis_data:/data

volumes:
  postgres_data:
  redis_data:

content.text: 14.2 CI/CD Pipeline — GitHub Actions

codeMap.yaml:
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

env:
  NODE_VERSION: '20'
  REGISTRY: ghcr.io
  IMAGE_NAME: ${{ github.repository }}

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test
          POSTGRES_DB: testdb
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready
          --health-interval 10s
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ env.NODE_VERSION }}
          cache: 'npm'
      
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run test:unit -- --coverage
      - run: npm run test:e2e
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:test@localhost:5432/testdb
      
      - uses: codecov/codecov-action@v3
  
  build-and-push:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
  
  deploy:
    needs: build-and-push
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to production
        run: |
          kubectl set image deployment/app \
            app=${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}
          kubectl rollout status deployment/app --timeout=5m

content.text: Interview Questions: DevOps

content.question: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling? When do you use each?
content.answer:
Vertical Scaling (Scale Up): Increase the resources of a single machine (more CPU cores, more RAM, faster SSD).
- Pros: Simple — no code changes, no distributed systems complexity
- Cons: Hardware limits exist. Single point of failure. Downtime needed to resize. Expensive at high end.
- Use for: Databases (easier than distributed DB), when you haven't yet exhausted vertical options, small applications

Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out): Add more machines running the same application behind a load balancer.
- Pros: Theoretically unlimited. No single point of failure. Cost-effective (commodity hardware). Can scale individual services independently.
- Cons: Application must be stateless (sessions in Redis, not memory). More complex. Need load balancer, service discovery.
- Use for: Stateless web servers, microservices, read-heavy workloads

Practical approach: Start vertical (simpler), switch to horizontal when you hit limits or need high availability.

content.text: This chapter consolidates the most commonly asked web development interview questions across all major companies — FAANG, top startups, and mid-size companies. Organized by topic with comprehensive answers and code examples.
15.1 Frontend Interview Questions

content.question: What is event delegation and why is it important?
What are Web Workers and when would you use them?
Explain the browser's same-origin policy and CORS.
content.answer:
Same-Origin Policy (SOP): Browsers prevent JavaScript on page A from making requests to a different origin than page A. Origin = protocol + hostname + port.
https://learnxchain.com:443 ≠ https://api.learnxchain.com:443 (different subdomain)
https://learnxchain.com ≠ http://learnxchain.com (different protocol)

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing): The server explicitly tells the browser which origins are allowed to make cross-origin requests via response headers.

Simple requests (GET, POST with form-data): Browser adds `Origin: https://learnxchain.com`. Server must respond with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://learnxchain.com` (or *). If missing → browser blocks the response.

Preflight requests: For requests with custom headers, JSON bodies, or non-GET/POST methods, browser first sends OPTIONS request. Server responds with allowed methods, headers, and max cache time for preflight. Then browser sends actual request.

Credentials (cookies): Requires both `credentials: 'include'` on fetch AND `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` with a non-wildcard origin.

content.text: 15.2 Backend & System Design Quick Questions

content.question: What is the difference between SQL JOINs?
content.answer:
INNER JOIN: Returns only rows where there is a match in BOTH tables. Non-matching rows from either table are excluded.
SELECT * FROM orders INNER JOIN users ON orders.user_id = users.id;
→ Only orders with a valid user_id that exists in users table

LEFT JOIN: Returns ALL rows from the LEFT table, with matching rows from right table. If no match in right table → NULL values.
→ All orders, with user info if available (orders with deleted users still appear)

RIGHT JOIN: Opposite of LEFT JOIN. All rows from RIGHT table.
→ All users, even those with no orders

FULL OUTER JOIN: All rows from BOTH tables. NULLs where no match.
→ Combination of LEFT and RIGHT JOIN results

CROSS JOIN: Cartesian product — every row from table A combined with every row from table B. 10 × 10 = 100 rows.
→ Generating all combinations (rare, usually accidental)

SELF JOIN: Join a table with itself using an alias.
→ Hierarchical data: employees.manager_id references employees.id

content.question: What is the CAP Theorem?
content.answer:
CAP Theorem (Eric Brewer, 2000): A distributed data system can only guarantee 2 of 3 properties simultaneously:

C — Consistency: Every read receives the most recent write or an error. All nodes see the same data at the same time.

A — Availability: Every request receives a response (not necessarily with the latest data). The system is always operational.

P — Partition Tolerance: The system continues operating even if network partitions (message loss between nodes) occur.

In reality, network partitions ALWAYS happen — so it's always CP vs AP:

CP (Consistent + Partition Tolerant): Returns error rather than stale data. Use for: banking, payment systems (ZooKeeper, HBase, MongoDB in default mode)

AP (Available + Partition Tolerant): Returns best-effort data that may be stale. Use for: DNS, social feeds, product catalog (Cassandra, CouchDB, DynamoDB)

CAP is often oversimplified — PACELC theorem extends it to also consider latency vs consistency tradeoffs during normal operation.
